articles.title: Ghost Data Still Exists: Building a Zero-Token Deletion-Audit Agent for GDPR Compliance
articles.excerpt: Under GDPR Article 17 and CCPA, users have the legal Right to be Forgotten. When a customer submits an account deletion request, the enterprise deletion workflow executes across services and returns a…
articles.body: Under GDPR Article 17 and CCPA, users have the legal Right to be Forgotten . When a customer submits an account deletion request, the enterprise deletion workflow executes across services and returns a status: status: COMPLETE Here is the ugly truth in enterprise engineering: In modern distributed systems, that COMPLETE status is often a dangerous illusion. Personal data doesn't just live in one tidy PostgreSQL table. It lingers in: Read replicas and reporting databases with asynchronous replication lag. Search engine clusters (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) holding denormalized user documents. Customer export bundles and support ticket attachments archived in object storage. Active data pipelines and backup restores that silently resurrect deleted records at 2:00 AM.

articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I co-founded NxFlowAI, an AI automation agency. Examples are generic. Small UK firms often run one shared inbox: info@, hello@, enquiries@. Three people read it, and now an automation draf…
articles.body: Disclosure: I co-founded NxFlowAI, an AI automation agency. Examples are generic. Small UK firms often run one shared inbox: info@, hello@, enquiries@ . Three people read it, and now an automation drafts replies too. The classic failure is the double reply: two staff answer the same customer with different prices, or a person answers while the bot's draft also goes out. For AI automation agency builds for UK small-business inboxes , the pattern I recommend is an ownership lock. Here is the design. The problem, stated precisely A thread can be touched by several actors: humans in the mail client, an automation drafting replies, and sometimes a CRM sequence. None of them knows the others are working. You need a shared notion of "who owns this thread right now".

articles.title: Make your RAG say 'I don't know': a score threshold, measured
articles.excerpt: A RAG system always gets something back from the index. Ask it about cooking and it returns the five nearest chunks of API docs, and the LLM then tries to be helpful. So: can a simple score threshold…
articles.body: A RAG system always gets something back from the index. Ask it about cooking and it returns the five nearest chunks of API docs, and the LLM then tries to be helpful. So: can a simple score threshold on retrieval tell "the docs cover this" from "they don't"? Short answer: yes, mostly. On the FastAPI docs, the top-1 cosine score separated the two groups well (AUC 0.986), and a threshold of 0.40 refused 24 of 30 unanswerable questions while answering 29 of 30 answerable ones. The leftovers are near-domain questions, which no threshold fully fixes. Raw BM25 scores did worse, and BM25 almost never returns an empty result. Setup Corpus: 152 files of the FastAPI docs, split into 2,808 heading-aware chunks with the heading path prefixed.

By targeting DNS resolution, the government aims to make the affected sites unreachable for most users without altering the underlying infrastructure of the platforms themselves.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
